S07.asr: Her check grew, but prices grew more, so today it buys less than her first check did. If her first check bought 10 crates of everything the index tracks, her check today buys about 9.

S24.asr: Ruth isn't the worst case. And she isn't the best. Carl, also illustrative, took the same kind of rising check in January 1966. His 20 years had the fastest price rise of any stretch, 6 .38 % a year. Like Ruth's, his first check bought a row of 10 crates. On every one of his 20 anniversaries, his check bought less than it had the year before. Ruth's check climbed back Back in her early years, Carl's never did.

S27.asr: Edna, also illustrative, started in January 1949, the last starting month, when a two percent raise kept up. Twenty years later, her check still bought at least what her first one did. She is part of that early handful, and nobody who started after her got that answer. Her twenty years ended a few years into Carl's. The same few years of prices came at the end of her stretch, with all ten crates It's still lit, and at the start of his.

S29.asr: Same raise, same rule. Edna kept up, Ruth fell short late, and Carl fell far behind. In crates, Edna's row ended full. Ruth set about nine, and Carl's at about four. What differed was the month each one started and what prices did after that.
